title: Systematic enumeration without missing cases
transcript: A complete list follows a rule you can explain. Fix one choice and list every possible ending before changing the first choice. When a list gets long, record a range or a subtotal for each first choice. This keeps the reason that the list is complete.

A late AMC counting question may hide a short list behind several conditions. Pick one condition that makes the list shrink quickly. In Mawa primary application practice, a complete list can be part of the answer. The published application questions ask students to explain their reasoning.
Use two different digits chosen from two, three and four. List all the possible two-digit numbers in increasing order. Think about which position decides the order first.

Start with tens digit two. The other two digits are the only possible ones digits, so write those endings in order. Repeat with each remaining tens digit. The complete list is twenty-three, twenty-four, thirty-two, thirty-four, forty-two and forty-three.
Two numbered counters A and B show whole numbers from one to eight. Their values sum to fourteen. How many possible ordered pairs of readings are there? A and B are distinct counters.
B equals fourteen minus A. Since B is at most eight, A must be at least six. The cap on A is eight. Every integer in that inclusive range gives one legal B, for three pairs.

Three labelled boxes A, B and C contain a total of twelve tokens. Each holds between one and seven tokens inclusive. A holds an even number. Count the different ordered triples of box sizes. The boxes keep their labels.

The possible values for A are two, four and six. Make a row for each one. In each row B plus C is twelve minus A. Requiring C to be at most seven gives a lower bound on B. Requiring C to be positive gives the upper bound. Use the cap of seven on B as well, then count the range inclusively.

The row counts are five, seven and five, so there are seventeen triples altogether. Each legal triple has exactly one value for A. Within that row a legal B fixes C, so every triple is covered exactly once.

An inclusive range includes both endpoints. Subtract first from last and then add one, provided the range is nonempty. When the boxes are labelled, swapping two different readings changes the triple. Retain the positions while you count.
Find a first choice whose legal values fit in a short list. Label the rows with those values. Write why each row covers its legal endings. Check both endpoints and add the disjoint row totals.
